description:
We are 'The Ripple Effect', a team of data-driven builders fascinated by the hidden patterns in Earth observation data. 

Who we are: A multidisciplinary squad consisting of Computer Science, Data Science, and Engineering undergraduates passionate about uncovering hidden patterns in complex systems.
summary:
Counterpoint: Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive dashboard that turns NASA Earth-system data into trend maps, each graded for how far it can be trusted. Using real GRACE/GRACE-FO water-storage data, it shows what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is significant. Every location gets a Theil-Sen slope with a 95% interval and a Mann-Kendall test, then a grade: A (robust), B (fragile), C (indistinguishable from noise) or D (possible artifact of the 2017-18 mission gap). Optional layers add rainfall, temperature, soil wetness and wildfire data from NASA POWER/MERRA-2 and FIRMS.


A variable can trend up in one region and down in another, so our mirror finder ranks opposite-sign region pairs and checks whether precipitation follows or opposes each split (association, not cause). A benchmark scorecard tests the tool against regions in NASA’s published findings, with the region list frozen beforehand and misses shown as prominently as hits. A Cross-check page re-tests trends on independent Giovanni, Hydrology Time Series or KNMI exports.


It matters because 20 years of data is easily over-read. Counterpoint shows students and the public how strong the evidence is, and where it runs out.
details:
1. WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Counterpoint: Earth System Trend Detective is a Python and Streamlit dashboard. It takes NASA Earth-system data, finds trends across the land surface, and grades each trend by how much evidence supports it. For each location it answers the challenge’s four questions (what is changing, where, by how much, and is it significant) and adds a fifth: how far the answer can be trusted.

The data. The primary layer is JPL GRACE/GRACE-FO Mascon RL06.3 (CRI-filtered), which measures liquid water equivalent thickness. It has about 4,551 equal-area 3-degree mascons published on a 0.5-degree grid, covering 2002 onward. The loader reads the native mascon-ID layer and falls back to approximate 3-degree blocks if that layer is missing, and it reports which one it used. Optional layers are NASA POWER/MERRA-2 variables (rainfall, soil wetness, evaporation, temperature, humidity, wind), NASA FIRMS fire detections for a user-chosen bounding box, and a GRACE-minus-GLDAS groundwater-style anomaly.

The statistics, in order:

  1. Deseasonalise by subtracting each calendar month’s mean.
  2. Annual means. A year counts only if it has at least 9 months of data, so the 2017-18 mission-gap years drop out and only complete years are used (through 2025). Peak-season fire series require only their 3 months. We test annual means because month-to-month values are strongly linked, and testing them directly would overstate certainty.
  3. Mann-Kendall test (tie-corrected) for significance.
  4. Theil-Sen slope with a Sen/Gilbert 95% interval for the rate of change.
  5. Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate control at q = 0.10 across the units of each feature, and again across merged regions.
  6. Robustness. The slope is recomputed for every start/end-year window of at least 10 years. Robustness is the share of windows whose sign matches the full-record trend.
  7. Gap-step test. A regression fits a trend plus a step after the gap (2017.5 to 2018.4) and tests the step.

The grade rules, applied in order, first match wins:

  • D if the gap-step p < 0.01 and the raw trend p < 0.05.
  • C if q ≥ 0.10.
  • A if q < 0.10 and at least 80% of windows agree on the sign.
  • B otherwise.

D is checked first, so a unit that would otherwise be A or B can still get D. It is a “check this one” flag, not proof of an artifact, because the test cannot tell an instrument offset from a real change that straddles the gap.

2. DESIGN DECISIONS AND HOW THE CONTROLS WORK

“Hide Antarctica and Greenland” checkbox (on by default)

  • It removes any unit south of 60°S, plus anything north of 60°N between 75°W and 10°W, a rough rectangle standing in for Greenland.
  • Over ice sheets, GRACE mostly records ice-mass loss rather than the land-water hydrology the rest of the map and the precipitation checks are about. The extreme values there also dominate the color scale and wash out everything else.
  • The MERRA-2 pipeline uses the identical filter, so those layers are never fetched for ice, and hiding the units keeps the map consistent with them.
  • It is a box, so it also hides Iceland and some Arctic Canada. Unticking it shows everything.

Color-range slider (80 to 100, default 95). The color scale is symmetric about zero and capped at that percentile of absolute slope, so a few extreme units do not turn the rest of the map one color.

Filters and presets. The evidence-grade filter defaults to A and B, and a direction filter offers Both, Rising or Falling. Region presets are World, Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania, Western USA and Mediterranean. World uses a Natural Earth projection and the regional presets zoom in. “Reset map view” re-centres the map.

Theme switch (Water or Wildfire conditions). Features are grouped so a student sees a coherent set of layers. Each feature carries a fire-direction tag, so the explanation text can say whether other variables are moving in a fire-promoting or fire-opposing direction.

Map encoding. Color shows the trend’s sign and size. Marker shape shows the grade (circle A, diamond B, square C, X D), so meaning never depends on color alone. Clicking a point enlarges it and fades the rest. A “Find a Location” dropdown, sorted by largest trend first, stays synced with the map click, which also helps keyboard and mobile users.

Place names. A selected point is reverse-geocoded through OpenStreetMap’s Nominatim. The client is limited to 1 request per second, as the public server requires, results are cached for 24 hours, and the lookup runs only for the selected point.

Details panel. A fixed panel shows:

  • the trend with its 95% interval, and the change as a percentage of the average level per decade where that makes sense
  • significance after FDR control, with p, q, percentage of windows agreeing, years used and gap-step p
  • the grade and its plain-English reason
  • the mirror-pair summary
  • rule-based “what may be behind it” notes, labelled association, not cause
  • a table of every other loaded feature at that location

Nearest unit within 700 km. Features sit on different grids (POWER is sampled every other 3-degree block), so cross-feature comparisons and the Cross-check page match to the nearest unit and refuse anything farther than 700 km.

Mirror-pair rules

  • Same-sign A/B units within 500 km merge into regions. Each region’s averaged series is re-tested and re-graded as one series.
  • A mirror pair is a rising A/B region and a falling A/B region within 6,000 km.
  • Pairs are ranked by the smaller of the two |slope| / standard-error ratios, so a pair is only as strong as its weaker side.
  • The top 10 pairs get a driver check against annual MERRA-2 precipitation at each region’s centre. The label is “follows” or “opposes”, or “unreliable” if the precipitation trend has p ≥ 0.10. A plain-English verdict is generated from the two labels.
  • The page also lists which other features split the same way across the pair.

Feature-specific choices

  • Vapor pressure deficit is derived from MERRA-2 temperature and humidity with a saturation-vapor-pressure formula.
  • Fire detections are counted per 3-degree block per month and mapped to the nearest GRACE unit within 400 km. Units with fewer than 12 detections in total are dropped.
  • “Peak-season fire detections” keeps only each unit’s three consecutive highest-climatology months, so the off-season does not dilute the trend.
  • The groundwater-style anomaly sums GLDAS soil layers, snow water equivalent and canopy water, converts kg/m² to cm, and re-baselines to 2004-2009 before subtracting from GRACE. Surface water and reservoirs are not removed, so it is labelled indicative only.
  • The fire layer queries FIRMS in 10-day windows (about 880 requests per bounding box), caches each window, and waits and retries on rate-limit errors.

Downloads. Map data can be downloaded as CSV or GeoJSON. In the GeoJSON each unit is drawn as a 3° × 3° square around its centroid, which approximates the true mascon shape.

Benchmark scoring. The tool is tested against regions described in NASA’s “Human Fingerprint on Earth’s Water Cycle” story. Each pre-listed region is scored as:

  • recovered (expected sign and grade A or B)
  • recovered (fragile) (grade B)
  • contradicted
  • missed (not distinguishable from noise)
  • unreliable (gap artifact)

A region expected to show no trend counts as recovered only if it is graded C. The region file’s SHA-256 and its frozen flag are stored with every run and shown in the app, with a warning if the list was not frozen. Misses are shown as prominently as hits.

3. PAGES AND RESILIENCE

  • Home: map, details panel, inspector (time series, trend line, gap band, window-robustness heatmap), mirror cases, benchmark scorecard, methods and limits.
  • Data: browse and download results, regional summaries, mirror pairs and raw monthly series. It reloads when a run rewrites the files.
  • Cross-check: the user uploads a monthly series from Giovanni, Hydrology Time Series or KNMI Climate Explorer, and the same engine runs on it unchanged. The page reports direction, interval overlap and annual correlation, and requires at least 10 overlapping annual means. Every comparison, including disagreements, is saved, and a repeat of the same tool, feature and point replaces the earlier row.
  • Methods, User Guide and Credits: full method, glossary, troubleshooting and attribution.
  • One-command, resumable pipeline: streamlit run app.py starts a background thread that downloads GRACE, grades the trends, registers the results and fetches the optional layers. A live progress page updates itself. A feature counts as ready only when results.csv exists and meta.json (written last) parses, so half-written files never appear. A failed required step stops setup with a Retry button, and a failed optional step is marked unavailable while the rest carries on. The FIRMS key is masked in the log, and analysis is spread across CPU cores.

4. BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

  • For students and the public: every number appears with its grade, and each chart has a “What you’re seeing / Why it matters” box. The glossary and user guide support learners who are not specialists.
  • For critical thinking: it shows uncertainty, reports misses as prominently as hits, separates association from cause, and checks itself against independent sources.
  • For educators and researchers: all outputs are downloadable, and new variables can be added with one entry in the feature catalog.
  • Intended impact: to make people more careful about what about 20 years of satellite data can and cannot say, and to show that student-built software can turn raw planetary data into verifiable, honestly graded insight.

5. TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

  • Language and app: Python, Streamlit (multipage navigation, caching, auto-refreshing fragments, custom CSS).
  • Analysis: NumPy, pandas, SciPy, xarray, netCDF4, pymannkendall (Hamed-Rao cross-check).
  • Visualization: Plotly (maps, charts, heatmap), Matplotlib.
  • Data access: earthaccess (NASA Earthdata), Requests (POWER and FIRMS), geopy (Nominatim).
  • Testing: pytest regression tests, a synthetic calibration command, and an Earthdata connectivity script.
  • Data: NASA/JPL GRACE and GRACE-FO (PO.DAAC), MERRA-2 via NASA POWER, MODIS fire detections via NASA FIRMS, GLDAS-Noah 2.1 (GES DISC), Giovanni, Hydrology Time Series, KNMI Climate Explorer, and OpenStreetMap.
  • Hardware: an ordinary laptop. No GPU is needed.

6. WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

  • Uncertainty is the product: a four-grade evidence system sits next to every number, including a grade for mission-gap artifacts.
  • It tackles the challenge’s “opposite directions” idea directly, with an automated mirror finder and an honest association-only driver check.
  • It audits itself with a hashed, freezable benchmark, FDR control and equal prominence for misses.
  • It has a built-in independent cross-check that reuses the exact same engine on external exports.
  • One engine runs water, climate, reanalysis and fire layers.
  • A synthetic validate command plants noise, true trends and gap steps to check how the grading behaves. It is labelled synthetic and never feeds the app.

7. FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

  • Scientific honesty: GRACE measures total water storage, not groundwater. Mascons are about 3° wide. Two decades can mistake natural cycles for trends. Year-to-year dependence is not fully corrected, so p-values can be somewhat optimistic. Spatially correlated neighbors make q-values approximate. The precipitation driver is a single point per region. MERRA-2 is model output. Fire detections are not burned area. Cross-checks are consistency checks on chosen points, not ground truth, and the products may share inputs. Everything is association, not cause.
  • Data integrity: real data only in the app, and synthetic data only in labeled validation. The benchmark list is hashed on every run so any change to it is visible.
  • Engineering: the riskiest step (opening the real GRACE file) was done first, with a defined fallback order. Rate limits, large downloads and half-written files are handled by caching, resumable steps and opt-in toggles. Automated Hydrology Time Series fetching was dropped because the service returned an HTML page to scripts, so the cross-check uses real exported files.
  • Usability and security: plain definitions, shape and color together, back buttons, troubleshooting, and opt-in credential storage with a plain-text warning.
  • Compliance: NASA does not endorse non-U.S. Government entities, and we follow each source’s data-use terms.

Team: Aanya Tiwari (Project Lead, Backend, Pipeline), Dat Hoang Vien (Frontend, DevOps), Swapnil Tiwari (Strategist), Tuhina Tiwari (Coordinator).
